name: Cybercrime & Internet Measurement
description: Empirical measurement of cybercrime, underground economies, abuse, fraud, and large-scale internet ecosystems.

uss.narrative:
The earliest papers in this list (all USENIX Security 2018) show cybercrime and internet measurement spreading across several distinct fronts at once. On the financial side, "An Empirical Analysis of Anonymity in Zcash" (USENIX 2018) probed whether a privacy-focused cryptocurrency actually delivered its promised anonymity, while "Plug and Prey? Measuring the Commoditization of Cybercrime via Online Anonymous Markets" (USENIX 2018) measured how attack capabilities were becoming off-the-shelf commodities. In parallel, the email/abuse front opened with "End-to-End Measurements of Email Spoofing Attacks" (USENIX 2018), and the measurement infrastructure front advanced with "Quack: Scalable Remote Measurement of Application-Layer Censorship" (USENIX 2018), which extended global censorship detection beyond DNS and IP blocking. From the start the area was empirical and data-driven rather than theoretical.

By 2019 the field sharpened around two themes: software supply-chain risk and email-borne fraud. "Small World with High Risks: A Study of Security Threats in the npm Ecosystem" (USENIX 2019) became a heavily cited template for treating a package registry as an attack surface, while a cluster of enterprise-fraud papers — "Detecting and Characterizing Lateral Phishing at Scale" and "High Precision Detection of Business Email Compromise" (both USENIX 2019) — shifted phishing research from generic spam toward targeted, high-value impersonation. Threat-intelligence itself came under measurement scrutiny in "Reading the Tea leaves: A Comparative Analysis of Threat Intelligence" (USENIX 2019), a skeptical-empiricism turn that continued into "A different cup of TI? The added value of commercial threat intelligence" (USENIX 2020).

Around 2019-2021 the center of gravity moved strongly toward two engines: the phishing lifecycle and blockchain/smart-contract abuse. "Sunrise to Sunset" and "PhishTime" (both USENIX 2020) measured the end-to-end effectiveness of the anti-phishing ecosystem and its blacklists, turning phishing into a longitudinal, defense-evaluation problem. Meanwhile Ethereum became its own underground economy to be measured: "The Art of The Scam: Demystifying Honeypots in Ethereum Smart Contracts" (USENIX 2019), "Frontrunner Jones and the Raiders of the Dark Forest" (USENIX 2021), and "Smart Contract Vulnerabilities: Vulnerable Does Not Imply Exploited" (USENIX 2021) — the last making the crucial point that measured exploitation matters more than theoretical vulnerability counts. The area also broadened beyond money to human harm with "The Tools and Tactics Used in Intimate Partner Surveillance" (USENIX 2020).

Most recently the work matures into ecosystem-scale economic studies and a new adversary. "A Large Scale Study of the Ethereum Arbitrage Ecosystem" (USENIX 2023) treats decentralized finance as a full economy to be quantified, and "Malla: Demystifying Real-world Large Language Model Integrated Malicious Services" (USENIX 2024) marks the arrival of LLM-powered cybercrime as a measurable underground market — closing the loop back to the 2018 commoditization theme, now with AI as the commodity.

top4.narrative:
The earliest papers in this list, all from 2018, show a field built around measuring how money, data, and abuse flow through real internet ecosystems. Several strands run in parallel. One follows the money into cryptocurrency: "Tracking Ransomware End-to-end" (S&P 2018) traced ransom payments through Bitcoin, while "An Empirical Analysis of Anonymity in Zcash" (USENIX 2018) showed that even a privacy coin's anonymity set was thinner than advertised, and a cluster of CCS 2018 papers ("MineSweeper", "How You Get Shot in the Back") documented the sudden rise of browser-based cryptojacking. A second strand measured the privacy and abuse economy directly, from the global mobile-tracking study (NDSS 2018) to "Plug and Prey?" (USENIX 2018), which quantified how cybercrime itself was being commoditized on anonymous markets. Email and account abuse rounded out the early work with "End-to-End Measurements of Email Spoofing Attacks" (USENIX 2018).

By 2019 the field broadened from "follow the money" to "measure the whole supply chain." Software-supply-chain and disclosure ecosystems came into focus with "Small World with High Risks: A Study of Security Threats in the npm Ecosystem" (USENIX 2019), "How Bad Can It Git?" (NDSS 2019) on leaked secrets, and a pair of papers on inconsistencies in public vulnerability reports (USENIX/NDSS 2019). IoT measurement matured from one-off curiosities into population studies with "All Things Considered: An Analysis of IoT Devices on Home Networks" (USENIX 2019) and the Hajime botnet analysis (NDSS 2019). Crucially, researchers also turned a skeptical eye on the tools defenders themselves rely on, with "Reading the Tea leaves: A Comparative Analysis of Threat Intelligence" (USENIX 2019) exposing how little overlap and reliability those feeds had. Phishing became a measurement discipline of its own, beginning with "PhishFarm" (S&P 2019) and "Detecting and Characterizing Lateral Phishing at Scale" (USENIX 2019).

Around 2020 the field consolidated two new pillars: rigorous longitudinal measurement and ecosystem-scale infrastructure. The phishing line matured into the end-to-end lifecycle and continuous-measurement studies "Sunrise to Sunset" and "PhishTime" (both USENIX 2020), while "Measuring and Modeling the Label Dynamics of Online Anti-Malware Engines" (USENIX 2020) questioned the VirusTotal labels everyone had been trusting. Internet-scale observatories like "Censored Planet" (CCS 2020) and "ICLab" (S&P 2020) turned censorship into a continuously monitored global signal, and regulation-driven measurement arrived with cookie-banner compliance under GDPR (S&P 2020). The field also widened its definition of harm beyond fraud, with "The Tools and Tactics Used in Intimate Partner Surveillance" (USENIX 2020) bringing interpersonal abuse into scope.

Most recently, blockchain and decentralized finance have become the center of gravity. After early curiosities like Ethereum honeypots (USENIX 2019), the work grew quantitative and systemic: "Frontrunner Jones and the Raiders of the Dark Forest" (USENIX 2021) and the landmark "Quantifying Blockchain Extractable Value: How dark is the forest?" (S&P 2022) named and measured MEV as a structural form of value extraction, while "Understanding Security Issues in the NFT Ecosystem" (CCS 2022) and the EIP-1559 fee analysis (CCS 2022) measured emerging crypto markets and protocol changes. In parallel the community produced systematizing and field-experiment work that reframes whole problems, from "SoK: Hate, Harassment, and the Changing Landscape of Online Abuse" (S&P 2021) to the real-organization field study "Phishing in Organizations" (S&P 2022). The throughline across all four venues is a steady move from measuring single scams toward measuring entire economies, infrastructures, and human-harm ecosystems at scale.
